podcast.title: Cult Status and Influence
podcast.body: The Cramps, with Poison Ivy at its core alongside her husband and frontman Lux Interior, became a cult favorite that continues to influence subsequent generations of guitarists, both male and female, as evidenced by bands like Queens of the Stone Age. "And in the process, the Cranps became this weird cult favorite that is still having an impact today. As Queens of the Stone Age, what they think of Ivy."

podcast.title: Early Guitar Playing
podcast.body: Poison Ivy, whose real name is Kristi Marlena Wallace, originated from California and began playing the guitar at an early age. "She was originally from California and started playing the guitar early."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Style and Contribution to The Cramps
podcast.body: Poison Ivy, real name Christie Wallace, was the guitarist and co-writer of all original songs for The Cramps, a New York City-based band known for its unique blend of punk, psychobilly, garage, and horror movie aesthetics. She also occasionally provided vocals and, despite not being a virtuoso, was an inspirational figure in a challenging music scene. "She co-wrote all the groups original songs and occasionally sang."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Meeting and Formation (Sacramento 1972-1975)
xref.body: Erick perkaiser (Lux interior) and Kristi Marlena Wallace (Poison Ivy) met in Sacramento in 1972. They were drawn together by a shared passion for horror movies and record collecting. By 1975, they had formed The Cramps and began performing at venues like CBGB, sharing stages with bands such as The Ramones, Blondie, Talking Heads, and Patti Smith. "They met in Sacramento back in 1972, and were drawn together by their love of horror movies and record collecting. By 1975, they'd formed the Cramps and were playing places like CBGB alongside their hormones and blondie and talking heads and patty smith and so many others."

xref.title: Enduring Core (Until 2006)
xref.body: While other members of The Cramps changed over time, Lux interior and Poison Ivy remained a constant, together recording and performing until 2006. "Other members of the Cramps came and went, but Lux and Poison Ivy stayed together recording and performing until 2006."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lux Interior's Death (February 4, 2009)
xref.body: Lux interior died suddenly on February 4, 2009, from an aortic dissection, an undiagnosed condition where the body's largest artery ruptures, leading to rapid internal bleeding. He and Poison Ivy had been married for 37 years. "But then on February 4th, 2009, Lux suddenly died after suffering an aortic dissection, an undiagnosed condition where your aorta, the largest artery in your body, bursts, and you bleed out internally in seconds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Absence of a Bass Player
xref.body: In the band's early days, The Cramps did not have a bass player, leaving it entirely up to guitarist Poison Ivy to handle the low-end duties and anchor the music. "Early on, the band didn't have a bass player. It was entirely up to Ivy to hold things down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band's End with Lux Interior's Death
xref.body: The Cramps disbanded after the death of singer Lux Interior in 2009 from an undiagnosed cardiovascular condition. Lux and Poison Ivy had been together for 37 years. "until Lux died of an undiagnosed cardiovascular condition in 2009. Now is the end of the band. Lux and Ivy had been together for 37 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Poison Ivy's Guitar Influence
xref.body: Poison Ivy's distinctive guitar style was considered a crucial influence on various aspects of the punk rock music scene. "Her guitar style was seen as an essential influence on certain areas of the punk rock universe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
